faq.q: Can a TIA cause permanent brain damage?

faq.q: Is anticoagulation ever used for TIA?

exam: What immediate investigations would you order for a patient with sudden unilateral weakness lasting 15 minutes? — Check glucose, non‑contrast CT, ECG, and arrange carotid imaging; each answers a specific differential.
How does the management differ between a large‑artery atherosclerotic TIA and a cardio‑embolic TIA? — Antiplatelet vs anticoagulation, plus need for carotid surgery in the former.

A patient with TIA has a carotid stenosis of 80 % but is awaiting surgery; what medical therapy should you start and why? — High‑dose aspirin plus statin to reduce recurrent risk; avoid clopidogrel dual therapy due to bleeding risk.
Explain why a normal CT does not exclude a recent stroke in a patient with transient symptoms. — CT is insensitive to early ischemia; MRI DWI would be needed, but may be unavailable.
What risk factor is most strongly associated with TIA in a young patient with sickle‑cell disease? — Sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusion causing cerebral ischemia; manage with transfusion and hydroxyurea.

How would you differentiate a TIA from a seizure with post‑ictal weakness at the bedside? — Seizure has positive motor activity, tongue biting, post‑ictal confusion; TIA has negative focal deficit without altered consciousness.
Why is blood pressure control critical after a TIA, and what target is recommended? — Prevent recurrent ischemia; aim for <140/90 mmHg (or <130/80 mmHg if diabetic).
In a resource‑limited hospital without MRI, what is the best strategy to risk‑stratify a TIA patient? — Use clinical ABCD2 score, bedside carotid duplex, and urgent CT to guide urgency of referral.
ai.title: Transient Ischemic Attack
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A brief, reversible neurologic deficit caused by temporary cerebral ischemia. Recognise risk factors, urgent assessment, and secondary prevention to avoid stroke.

b: Duration <1 hour (often <10 min)
No permanent deficit
Imaging shows no acute infarct
sections.p: A transient ischemic attack (TIA) is a focal neurologic deficit lasting <1 hour (often <10 min) with complete resolution and no infarction on imaging. It signals an imminent stroke risk.

b: Atherosclerotic large‑artery disease
Cardio‑embolic (e.g., rheumatic mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation)
Small‑vessel disease (lacunar)
Other (dissection, vasculitis, hypercoagulable states)
sections.p: TIA is a vascular event. Classify by aetiology (TOAST) and by vascular territory. In low‑resource settings, common precipitants include uncontrolled hypertension, HIV‑associated vasculitis, sickle‑cell crisis, and rheumatic heart disease emboli.

b: Urgent ABCs, glucose, blood pressure control
Start antiplatelet therapy within 24 h
Arrange carotid imaging within 2 weeks
sections.p: TIA is a medical emergency; the 48‑hour stroke risk is ~10 % and 90‑day risk ~15 %. Early identification allows rapid secondary‑prevention measures that halve stroke incidence.

t.b: Rule out hypoglycaemia as a mimic; normal >70 mg/dL, low <70 mg/dL
Exclude intracerebral haemorrhage; normal CT supports TIA, but may miss early infarct
Detect ≥70 % stenosis needing endarterectomy; if unavailable, refer for CTA/MRA when possible
Identify atrial fibrillation or other arrhythmias; treat cardio‑embolic source

t.a: Full blood count, renal function, lipid profile
t.b: Baseline for secondary‑prevention drugs; treat dyslipidaemia

b: If carotid stenosis ≥70 % and symptomatic → refer for endarterectomy
Statin therapy for all patients regardless of cholesterol level
Blood pressure target <140/90 mmHg (or <130/80 mmHg if diabetic)
Lifestyle: smoking cessation, diet, exercise
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, start antiplatelet therapy, control blood pressure, and address modifiable risk factors.

b: Seizure: positive symptoms (jerking) then post‑ictal weakness
Migraine aura: visual scintillations, gradual spread
Hypoglycaemia: improves with glucose
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic TIA include seizures with post‑ictal weakness, migraine aura, hypoglycaemia, and conversion disorder.

b: CT may miss small cortical infarcts
Carotid duplex may underestimate high‑grade stenosis in heavy calcification
sections.p: A normal CT does not rule out a recent infarct; MRI diffusion‑weighted imaging is more sensitive but may be unavailable.

b: Check for carotid bruit – suggests atherosclerosis
Listen for irregular pulse – atrial fibrillation
Assess for focal weakness, speech changes, visual field loss
sections.p: Exam focuses on vascular risk assessment, cardiac exam for murmurs, and neurologic localisation.

Missing atrial fibrillation on brief ECG
